Subject: Re: Comcast's 6 recipient per second limit

On Wed, Feb 13, 2008 at 05:32:34PM -0500, Vivek Khera wrote:

> 
> On Feb 13, 2008, at 2:50 PM, Victor Duchovni wrote:
> 
> >Yes, 2.5 adds support for per-destination rate limits. Really intended
> >for users of SOHO ISP MSAs, the fact that you have to do this for a  
> >major
> >ISP inbound MX host is rather sad.
> 
> I have a list of about a dozen remote sites (some ISPs, some  
> universities, some non-profits) for which we have to throttle  
> delivery.  I'm very keen on implementing 2.5 with proper rate limits  
> rather than faking it with concurrency limits.  Some of the ISPs  
> actually need low concurrency limits rather than just rate limits,  
> which is also a PITA.

One of the things I am looking for you (if are able) to test with 2.5
is the new self-tuning concurrency feedback controls described (in part)
in SCHEDULER_README.

Specifically, if the ISP gives immediate (421 banner or EHLO/HELO)
negative feedback on concurrency overshoot, and does not make that sticky
(no subsequent blackout time for new connections) Postfix 2.5 should
"converge" to the ISP's limits with the right feedback settings.

Convergence means that Postfix will mostly operate at the maximum allowed
concurrency but will periodically try "one more" connection. So a fraction
of mail may be deferred, but the fraction is much lower than with prior
releases.

The interesting parameter values are:

    smtp_destination_concurrency_negative_feedback = 1/20
    smtp_destination_concurrency_positive_feedback = 1/8

this should exhibit a defer rate of ~10% or less if the
destination's preferred concurrency limit is below the
smtp_destination_concurrency_limit.

You can get a lower defer rate (less than 1/15 messages) with:

    smtp_destination_concurrency_negative_feedback = 1/20
    smtp_destination_concurrency_positive_feedback = 1/15

but this may result in low concurrency for a site behind a single
load-balanced IP and and an ~50% connection failure rate. I doubt that
such sites are a real problem...

Both algorithms lead to slightly slower concurrency growth from a
cold start. This is likely fine, but I am interested in performance
comparisons.

-- 
	Viktor.
